newsitem.title: USA: U.S. agents search for clues at clinic blast site.
newsitem.headline: U.S. agents search for clues at clinic blast site.

text.p: Federal agents on Friday swarmed through wreckage left by two "powerful" bombs that exploded at a suburban office building housing an abortion clinic, as investigators renewed a plea for public help to find the culprit.

More than 100 state and federal agents were assigned to the case, 50 of them at the office complex where the two bombs exploded an hour apart on Thursday, sending at least six people to hospitals and injuring many more, authorities said.
"These were two very powerful bombs," U.S. Attorney Kent Alexander said. "To me, the most remarkable thing about this case thus far is that no one was killed."

Police maintained a cordon in a 100-yard (metre) radius around the building in the Atlanta suburb of Sandy Springs, stopping workers hoping to return to their jobs and media who attempted to retrieve equipment left behind in panic.

Alexander said authorities had a myriad of good leads from about 200 telephone calls to a toll-free bombing hotline, (888) ATF-BOMB, and implored the public to keep calling. "There are people out there who know who did this," he said.

At the blast scene, investigators stopped searching for additional devices, declaring the site secure, and instead concentrated on finding clues. ATF agents guided trained dogs through the area and other investigators could be seen stooping to examine bits of material and marking the location where they were found.

Investigators also were checking for links to last July's Centennial Olympic Park bombing in Atlanta which left two people dead and more than 100 injured. Alexander said there were similarities between the bombings, but also "many differences," and refused comment on the type of bomb used at the clinic.

A state investigator reported finding nails in an adjacent seven-story office building where plate-glass windows were blown out by the bombs. And Fox television affiliate WAGA, citing unnamed sources, reported Friday that the second bomb was "packed with nails" intended to become "deadly projectiles" when the device went off.
The blasts rocked a building housing the Atlanta Northside Family Planning Services centre -- the same clinic that was the target of Atlanta's last abortion clinic bombing 13 years ago.
Alexander said no arrests had been made and, to his knowledge, no one had claimed responsibility for the bombings.

The first bomb exploded about 9:30 a.m. EST (1430 GMT). An hour later, as law enforcement officials and firefighters sifted through debris, a second bomb detonated near a garbage container in the building's parking lot, injuring at least six people including agents from the FBI and ATF.

The clinic sees patients only on certain days and Thursday was not one of them, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported. Just three people were in the clinic when the first bomb went off. On a clinic day there might have been 15-20 employees as well as patients, the newspaper said.
Police stopped residents and workers near the clinic during the Friday morning rush hour, asking if they had seen anything suspicious the previous morning.

The two bombs caused extensive damage to the building and the second left a large crater near the garbage container. Alexander said it was fortunate that two cars parked near the second bomb had absorbed much of the force of the blast. One of the cars was "pretty much demolished," he said.
Local press reports said the FBI intended to scrutinise videotapes taken by security cameras at the building for clues.

Of the half dozen people who were taken to hospitals as a result of the blast, only one, an FBI agent, remained for tests. But Alexander said numerous other people had been "cut, scraped, bruised and traumatized by the bomb."
Local firefighters Friday offered a $15,000 reward for information in the bombing and said they would handle future calls more cautiously.
